name: Kullu Dussehra
when: October, starting on Vijayadashami and running seven days (lunar; dates move each year)
summary: Kullu's great autumn gathering begins on Vijayadashami, the day Dussehra ends elsewhere in India. For seven days, village deities carried in palanquins from across the valley assemble around Raghunath ji at Dhalpur Maidan in Kullu town, about 25 km from Naggar, the old capital of the Kullu rajas.
body: The festival grew around Raghunath ji, a form of Rama whose image was brought to Kullu from Ayodhya in the 17th century during the reign of Raja Jagat Singh. Tradition says the raja installed the image and declared Raghunath the true ruler of the valley, governing in the deity's name. Dussehra became the occasion on which the valley's many village gods, the devtas, come to pay their respects to him. Naggar, where the rajas ruled before moving down to Sultanpur in Kullu, keeps that older history in its castle and temples.

On the first afternoon, Raghunath ji is taken from his temple in Sultanpur to Dhalpur Maidan and placed on a wooden chariot, which crowds pull across the ground with ropes. Devtas arrive from villages across the Kullu valley and beyond, each in a palanquin carried on men's shoulders, with drums, long brass horns and a band of devotees. Hadimba Devi, the patron goddess of the Kullu royal family, comes down from her temple in Manali. Through the week, the deities sit in camps around the maidan and devotees move between them.

Dhalpur becomes a fair as well: stalls sell Kullu shawls and caps, woollens, utensils and food, and the evenings bring cultural programmes and the Kullu nati, the linked-arm circle dance of the valley. On the last day, the chariot is drawn to the bank of the Beas for the Lanka Dahan rite, and the devtas begin their walks home. The state celebrates it as International Kullu Dussehra, with visiting troupes on the stage at night.
tips: Stay in Naggar or Manali rather than Kullu town, where rooms fill and prices rise; buses and taxis to Dhalpur take about an hour.
Be at Dhalpur by early afternoon on the first day to see the chariot pulled; it gets very crowded, so keep children close.
Ask before photographing a devta's palanquin or its bearers, and never touch a palanquin or step through a procession.

faqs.a: It begins on Vijayadashami, the tenth day of the bright half of the lunar month of Ashvin, usually in October, and lasts seven days. Because it follows the lunar calendar, the date moves each year; check the current year's dates with Himachal tourism before you book rooms.

The main events take place at Dhalpur Maidan in Kullu town, on the Beas. Naggar is about 25 km and Manali about 40 km away, and both make calmer bases with regular buses and taxis into Kullu through the festival week.

faqs.q: Is Kullu Dussehra crowded, and is it safe?
faqs.a: It is very crowded, especially on the first and last days, with police and volunteers managing the ground. Pickpocketing happens, so keep valuables close. Families with small children are better off visiting the deity camps on a weekday morning in the middle of the week.

faqs.q: Do I need tickets for Kullu Dussehra?
faqs.a: No. Entry to Dhalpur Maidan and the deity camps is free. Some evening cultural programmes have reserved seating, but the ground and the processions are open to everyone. Hotel rooms are the real cost: book early, as rates rise for the festival week.

name: Minjar Mela, Chamba
when: July–August, about a week from the second Sunday of the month of Shravan (lunar)
summary: Chamba's week-long harvest fair in the monsoon month of Shravan. People wear the minjar, a tassel of silk and gold thread that recalls the flowering of maize, and the fair ends with a procession to the Ravi, where the minjar and offerings are given to the river.
body: Minjar is Chamba's own festival and one of the oldest fairs in Himachal. It falls in Shravan, when the maize in the fields of the Ravi valley is in tassel, and the minjar itself, a small tassel of silk and zari thread pinned to clothes, is a reminder of that crop. Families give minjars to each other at the start of the fair and wear them through the week. The minjar is also offered at the town's temples, including the Lakshmi Narayan group and the Raghuvira temple.

The fair takes place on the Chaugan, the long green in the middle of Chamba town. The opening is marked by the hoisting of the Minjar flag, and through the week the Chaugan fills with stalls, rides, sports and evening programmes of Himachali music and dance. Traders bring Chamba chappals, rumals and metalwork, and villagers come in from the surrounding valleys.

On the final day a procession with drums and the images of the deities moves from the town to the bank of the Ravi. There, the minjars are offered to the river together with a coconut, a rupee and other offerings, a gesture of thanks for the harvest and a prayer for the rains. Kunjri-malhar, the traditional monsoon songs of the Chamba hills, are sung during the festival. It is a family occasion more than a spectacle, and visitors are welcome to watch and join the crowd on the Chaugan.
tips: Buy a minjar from a stall on the first day and wear it; it costs little and people notice.
Shravan is monsoon season; the roads from Pathankot and Dharamshala can be blocked by slides, so keep a buffer day and check current status before you travel.
Visit the Bhuri Singh Museum near the Chaugan during the fair to see Chamba rumals and Pahari miniatures in context.

faqs.q: When is the Minjar Mela in Chamba?
faqs.a: It usually starts on the second Sunday of the Hindu month of Shravan, in late July or early August, and runs for about a week. The exact dates are announced each year by the district administration; check current status before you travel.

A minjar is a small tassel of silk and gold thread worn on clothes during the festival. It recalls the tassels of the maize crop, which flowers at this time, and is exchanged between family and friends and finally offered to the Ravi on the last day.

faqs.q: Is it safe to travel to Chamba in the monsoon for Minjar?
faqs.a: The town itself is fine, but the roads in can be hit by landslides and delays of several hours are common. Travel in daylight, use HRTC buses or an experienced driver, and keep a spare day in your plan.

faqs.q: Where should I stay during the Minjar Mela?
faqs.a: Stay in Chamba town, close to the Chaugan, so you can walk to the evening programmes. HPTDC and small hotels fill during the fair, so book a few weeks ahead. Dalhousie, about 2 hours away, is an alternative if Chamba is full.

name: Losar in McLeodganj
when: February or March, from the first day of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar
summary: Tibetan New Year in the exile capital. Families clean their homes, eat guthuk soup on the eve, fry khapse biscuits and hang new prayer flags, while monks hold prayers at the Tsuglagkhang complex. The main celebration lasts three days; shops and cafés close for part of it.
body: Losar marks the start of the Tibetan year and follows the lunar calendar, so it falls in February or early March. In McLeodganj, home of the Central Tibetan Administration and a large Tibetan community since the 1960s, it is the biggest event of the year. Preparations begin days ahead: homes are cleaned, families fry khapse, crisp twisted biscuits, and kitchens prepare offerings for the altar.

Two days before the new year, families eat guthuk, a noodle soup with dough balls that hide small objects such as chilli, wool or salt; what you find in your bowl is read as a playful comment on your character for the coming year. The following day is given to rituals for clearing away the old year's obstacles. On Losar morning, people visit the temple and monasteries early, offer khata scarves and greet each other with Losar Tashi Delek.

Through the three days of celebration, new prayer flags go up on rooftops and on the hill paths around the Lingkor, the circuit around the Tsuglagkhang. Monks at the Tsuglagkhang complex and Namgyal Monastery hold prayers, and the community visits friends and family. For visitors, Losar means watching quietly, joining the circuit walk, and accepting that many Tibetan shops and restaurants close for a few days.
tips: Walk the Lingkor circuit early on Losar morning, clockwise, and keep to the side for people offering prayers.
Expect Tibetan-run cafés and shops to close on the main days; Indian-run dhabas and hotels stay open.
Dress modestly and ask before photographing people at prayer, and never during rituals inside the temple.

faqs.q: When is Losar celebrated in McLeodganj?
faqs.a: Losar falls on the first day of the first month of the Tibetan lunar calendar, usually in February or early March. The main celebration lasts three days. Dates change each year; check the Tibetan calendar or the Central Tibetan Administration's announcements before you travel.

faqs.q: Can tourists take part in Losar?
faqs.a: Yes, respectfully. Visitors can walk the Lingkor, visit the Tsuglagkhang complex and watch prayer-flag hanging. Celebrations are mostly family and community events, so do not expect staged shows. A simple Losar Tashi Delek greeting is always welcome.

faqs.q: Is February too cold for McLeodganj?
faqs.a: It is cold but manageable: days around 8–15 °C and nights near or below freezing, with occasional snow on the hills above. Bring warm layers; many guesthouses have limited heating, so ask for heaters or extra blankets.

faqs.q: Does the Dalai Lama appear during Losar?
faqs.a: Sometimes he leads prayers or teachings around the new year, but his schedule varies and he is not always in Dharamshala. Check the official schedule on his office's website before planning a trip around a public appearance.
